tagline: From rainforest to coast, a winding road repeatedly buried by lava
intro: Chain of Craters Road winds down from rainforest to the coast of Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park, descending 3,700 feet from Crater Rim Drive. The paved drive passes pit craters and lava flows; the National Park Service promotes it as a scenic drive and gives its present length as 18.8 miles. The route runs through Kīlauea’s East Rift and coastal country, with side paths leading to craters and other geological features.

Dedicated on April 15, 1928, the road, formerly Cockett’s Trail, originally ended at Makaopuhi crater. The coastal extension opened in 1965, only to be partly buried when the Maunaulu eruption began in 1969. A realigned road reopened in June 1979. Later, Puʻuʻōʻō lava covered nearly nine miles of road. In November 1992 it also buried the Kamoamoa village site, temple and black sand beach. Coastal trails, home sites, temples and agricultural sites record centuries of settlement, though lava has buried thousands of archaeological sites since 1969.

From the upper road, Pauahi Crater comes about three miles into the descent. Maunaulu marks the eruption that interrupted the coastal route. Farther toward the sea, the road crosses pāhoehoe lava. Near its end is the former site of Hōlei Sea Arch, which collapsed in late September 2026.

moments.title: Pauahi Crater
moments.text: Pauahi is a 300-foot-deep crater about three miles from the top of Chain of Craters Road. Its floor became an eruption site in May 1973, when a fissure opened and briefly released lava. That November, another eruption opened a series of fissures from west of the crater, across its floor and east toward Puu Huluhulu. The episode lasted 31 days, with most activity concentrated in its first ten hours. A third eruption, on November 16, 1979, lasted just one day. The crater measures 2,000 feet in length, with a width reaching up to some 1,300 feet.
moments.notice: Pauahi’s crater is 300 feet deep and 2,000 feet long.

moments.title: Maunaulu
moments.text: Maunaulu means “growing mountain,” a name borne out by the eruption that built this cone between May 1969 and July 1974. Lava from that eruption covered 44 square kilometers. At the time, it was Kīlauea’s longest-lasting and most voluminous flank eruption in at least 2,200 years. The road to the coast had opened in 1965; four years later, Maunaulu partly buried it. After the eruption, the road was realigned and reopened in June 1979. In 1,774 days the eruption produced 350 million cubic meters of lava, with flows running down the growing feature’s sides.

moments.title: Hōlei Sea Arch
moments.text: Hōlei Sea Arch once rose 90 feet above the southern coast near the road’s end. The National Park Service dates its lava flow to about 550 years ago and attributes the arch’s shape to waves eroding layers of different hardness at different rates. The original overlook closed in 2020 because of unstable cliffs. In 2022, a large surf event had already broken away part of the arch’s base. By the night of September 27, 2026, the arch had fallen. The park confirmed the collapse on October 1, but did not establish whether Hurricane Nolo’s surf or other storm conditions caused it.
